chapter.title: Adding the arms

cards.body:
You're lying on the water-bed, gliding with both arms out front. Now imagine grabbing a fistful of the sheet ahead of you and **pulling it back along your body**, so you slide forward over it.

One hand pulls under you while the other swings forward over the top to grab the next handful. That taking-turns is front crawl arms.
cards.simpler: Picture yourself lying flat on the water, both arms stretched out in front. Now imagine the water is a bedsheet. You grab a handful ahead of you and **pull it back along your body**, so you slide forward over it. While one hand pulls underneath, the other swings forward over the top to grab the next handful. The two hands take turns. That is what front crawl arms do.

cards.prompt: Maya is gliding in the shallow end, both arms stretched ahead. She wants her arms to move her forward. What should she do?

options.text: Pull both arms back under her at the same moment
Pull one arm back under her body while the other stays stretched ahead, then swap
Slap both hands up and down on the surface

whyNot.a: That's both hands grabbing the same handful of sheet, not taking turns: you get one shove, then nothing is reaching ahead to pull with.
whyNot.c: That's splashing the sheet, not pulling it: hands on the surface push nothing back, so you stay where you are.

cards.reteach: Picture pulling yourself along a mattress. You grab ahead with one hand and drag yourself past it, while the other hand is already reaching for the next grab. If both hands grab at once, you lurch forward once and then have to stop and reach again.

cards.title: One arm pulls
cards.body:
**One arm at a time.** Your right hand enters the water in front of your right shoulder, fingers first, like posting a letter through a slot. It presses down and back under your body, all the way past your hip. Then it lifts out.

Meanwhile your left arm stays stretched ahead, long and still, exactly like the front of your glide. Only when the right hand is finishing does the left one start to pull.

Practise this standing in chest-deep water, bent forward, chin just above the surface. Say it as you go: reach, pull, swap.
cards.simpler: **Only one arm moves at a time.** Your right hand slides into the water in front of your right shoulder, fingers first, like posting a letter through a slot. It pushes down and back under your body, past your hip, then lifts out. Your left arm stays stretched ahead, long and still, like in your glide. It only starts pulling as the right hand finishes. Practise standing in chest-deep water, bent forward, chin above the surface. Say reach, pull, swap.

cards.title: Tom and the dropped pencil
cards.body:
Tom tried his first 3 strokes from a push-off. His left arm did a lovely slow pull. His right arm, keen to help, pulled at exactly the same moment. He travelled about half a metre, then lay there with both arms by his sides like a dropped pencil, and stood up.

Next go, he told his right arm to wait its turn. 3 strokes became 2 metres.
cards.simpler: Tom tried his first 3 strokes after a push-off. His left arm did a lovely slow pull. His right arm wanted to help, so it pulled at exactly the same moment. He moved about half a metre. Then he lay there with both arms by his sides, like a dropped pencil, and stood up. On his next go, he **told his right arm to wait its turn**. The same 3 strokes carried him 2 metres.

cards.prompt: Priya pushes off, glides, kicks, and starts her arms. Her right hand is halfway through its pull under her body. What should her left arm be doing right now?

options.text: Stretched out in front, waiting its turn
Pulling too, so she goes twice as fast

whyNot.b: That's both arms grabbing at once, Tom's dropped-pencil move: one shove, then nothing out front to pull with.
whyNot.c: That's the end of a pull, not the wait: an arm by your side isn't ready to grab the next handful, and it lets your front sink.

cards.reteach: While one hand is pulling, the other is the front of your glide: long, still, pointing where you want to go. It starts its own pull only as the first hand finishes by your hip. One pulls, one waits, then they swap.

cards.title: The other arm comes back over the top
cards.body:
When your hand finishes by your hip, lift the elbow so it leads, let the hand hang loose, and swing it forward above the water to land in front of your shoulder again. Swimmers call this the *recovery*. It lifts nothing. **It's just travelling back for the next pull**, low and relaxed.

Keep the kick going underneath, small and steady, face in, breathing out.

Build it in steps. Push off, glide, 3 strokes, stand. When 3 feels calm, go to 6. Slow long strokes beat fast short ones: aim for about 1 second per pull.
cards.simpler: When your hand reaches your hip, lift the elbow so it leads, hand loose, and swing it forward over the water to land in front of your shoulder. This is called the recovery. **It is just the arm travelling back for the next pull**, low and relaxed. Keep the kick small and steady, face in, breathing out. Push off, glide, 3 strokes, stand. When 3 feels calm, try 6. Slow long strokes beat fast short ones, about 1 second each.

cards.body: Sam managed 6 strokes but arrived gasping, arms windmilling at double speed, hands slapping the water flat. The faster he churned, the less he moved. You can spot it from the poolside: **lots of splash, little travel**. The fix is counting out loud, one slow 'one' per pull, and letting the glide between strokes do some of the work.
cards.simpler: Sam got through 6 strokes but arrived out of breath. His arms were spinning round at double speed and his hands slapped flat on the water. The faster he churned, the less he moved. You can spot this from the side of the pool: **lots of splash, little travel**. The fix is to count out loud, one slow 'one' for each pull, and let the glide between strokes do some of the work.

cards.prompt: A friend asks what the arms actually do in front crawl. Which is the best one-line answer?

options.text: Both arms sweep back at the same time, like opening curtains
One arm pulls back under your body while the other swings forward over the water, and they take turns
Your hands paddle at the surface to keep your head up

whyNot.a: That's both arms at once: crawl arms take turns, so one is always pulling while the other is reaching.
whyNot.c: That's Sam's splash, not the pull: hands at the surface push nothing back. The pull happens under your body, and your face stays in.

cards.reteach: Think of the mattress again. One hand grabs ahead and drags you past it, under your body to your hip. The other swings over the top to grab the next handful. Pull under, recover over, swap, slowly.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Front crawl arms take turns**: one hand reaches in and pulls back under your body past your hip, while the other swings forward over the water to reach again. Keep it slow, keep the kick small, and build from 3 strokes to 6 before you ask for more.
cards.simpler: **Front crawl arms take turns.** One hand reaches in and pulls back under your body, past your hip. At the same time the other arm swings forward over the water, ready to reach in again. Keep it slow. Keep the kick small. Build from 3 strokes to 6 before you ask your arms for more.

cards.body: Tonight, out of the water: stand bent forward, hands stretched ahead as in a glide. Pull one hand back to your hip, swing it forward over the top, then the other. 10 slow turns, saying reach, pull, swap.
cards.simpler: Tonight, away from the pool, stand up and bend forward. Stretch both hands out ahead as if you were gliding. Pull one hand back to your hip, then swing it forward over the top. Now do the same with the other hand. Do **10 slow turns**, saying reach, pull, swap as you go.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now swim 6 to 8 front crawl strokes from a push-off, face in, arms taking turns, and stand up calmly.
